# On the Peculiar Joy of Small Inefficiencies

I've been thinking about how much time I spend looking for my keys. It's genuinely inefficient—I could install a hook by the door, use an AirTag, develop a system. Yet there's something oddly pleasant about the search itself.

It forces a small reset. While hunting through jacket pockets and under mail stacks, my mind wanders productively. I notice things: that plant needs water, I should call my friend, this book looked interesting. The friction of the search creates space for actual thinking, the kind that doesn't happen when I'm optimized into constant productivity.

Modern life optimizes away these moments. We streamline everything until there's no dead time, no gaps where our minds can roam. We've solved so many problems that we've accidentally eliminated some of the texture that made life interesting.

I wonder if this applies to bigger things. We rush to eliminate all difficulty, all inconvenience. But maybe some friction is feature, not bug. The conversation that meanders teaches you things a direct exchange wouldn't. The inefficient hobby—knitting, gardening, woodworking—succeeds because it resists optimization.

This isn't an argument against progress. Having reliable electricity is better than the romance of candlelight. Antibiotics beat contemplative suffering every time.

But somewhere between complete chaos and perfect efficiency lies actual life. It's found in the small moments where things don't work exactly as planned, where you have to slow down.

Maybe I'll get that hook eventually. But I'm in no rush.
